$comment: What a saved dashboard is, on the wire and on disk.
src/lib/dashboards/layout.test.ts both read this file. A layout written by
one and refused by the other is the failure it exists to prevent: the
console is not the only client (the phone loads the same console), and a
layout is the one piece of state a user builds by hand and would be angry
Coordinates are a 12-column grid. `w`/`h` are in columns and rows; a row is
whatever height the console draws it at, which is a display decision and

fields.title: what the user called it
fields.owner: the token id that saved it — see `owner` below
fields.widgets: array, in no particular order; `x`/`y` decide the layout
fields.range: the window the dashboard opens on: 1h | 6h | 24h | 7d

fields.title: optional; the series' own label is used when absent
fields.source: a data source name: internal | influx | …
fields.series: array of series keys, as that source lists them
fields.aggregate: last | mean | min | max | sum | count

types.area: the same, filled — for a quantity rather than a level
types.stat: one number, large, with an optional sparkline
types.table: several series' latest values, side by side

$comment: There are no user accounts (jarvis/auth.py:3). A token IS the identity:
one per device, minted by the operator. So a dashboard belongs to the
token that saved it, and 'per user' means 'per token id'. A layout with no
owner is shared — the shipped examples are.

commands.jarvis/dashboards/list: every dashboard this token may see: its own, plus the shared ones
commands.jarvis/dashboards/save: create or replace one; the server stamps `owner` from the token
commands.jarvis/dashboards/delete: by id; refuses one this token does not own
commands.jarvis/metrics/sources: what can be graphed, per source
